desc:
Stones lie on distinct integer points of a plane; the entry [x, y] of stones is a stone in column x and row y. In one move you may remove a stone s if at least one other stone that is still on the plane shares its column (same x) or its row (same y) with s.

Return the largest number of stones that can be removed by a sequence of such moves.

stones = [[0,0],[0,2],[1,1],[2,0],[2,2]]

result = 3

The four corner stones are linked through shared rows and columns, so three of them can go, while the middle stone has nobody in its row or column and must stay.
constraints: All stones are at different points
hints: Try small cases by hand: which stones can never be removed? Think about a stone that is alone in both its row and its column.
Consider the graph where two stones are linked when they share a row or a column. In a connected group, how many stones can you remove?

In every connected group all stones except one can be removed (always remove a leaf of a spanning tree first). So the answer is stones - groups. Count the groups with union-find by joining each stone's row and column.
editorial: Look at each connected group of stones, where two stones are neighbours if they share a row or a column. Inside one group, take a spanning tree and remove stones from the leaves inward: a leaf always still has its tree parent in its row or column, so it is removable. Everything except the last stone (the root) can therefore be removed. A lone stone cannot be removed at all. Hence the maximum is len(stones) - number_of_groups.

To count groups without building the stone graph (which could have O(n²) edges), treat every distinct row and every distinct column as a node and union x with y for each stone. Stones sharing a row or column end up in the same set. Offset the row ids (for example use ~y) so they never collide with column ids. Count the distinct roots among the stones. Time is O(n · α(n)).
